name: Rusfertide
summary: Rusfertide is now an FDA-approved treatment for erythrocytosis in adults with polycythemia vera, marketed as Mimrylo. It mimics hepcidin to restrict iron availability for red-cell production. Approval in August 2026 supersedes older descriptions that list it only as investigational.
description: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disease in which excessive red-cell production can require repeated therapeutic phlebotomy and other treatment. Rusfertide targets iron regulation rather than directly eliminating the underlying abnormal cell clone. By mimicking hepcidin, it reduces the iron supply available for erythropoiesis and helps control hematocrit. Earlier REViVE findings led to the phase 3 VERIFY program and US approval of Mimrylo on August 28, 2026. Its approved indication is erythrocytosis in adults with polycythemia vera. This should not be broadened to general blood donation replacement, every cause of high hematocrit, iron overload, or treatment of anemia.
mechanism: Rusfertide inhibits ferroportin, the transporter that moves iron from cells into circulation, reproducing a central action of endogenous hepcidin. Reduced iron availability to the marrow limits red-cell production and lowers hematocrit. This is iron redistribution and restriction of erythropoiesis, not destruction of mature red cells. The mechanism also explains why blood counts and anemia require monitoring and why the drug does not itself eradicate the PV clone.
keyTakeaway: Rusfertide has moved from clinical development into approved US care for a specific PV indication. Its benefit is hematocrit control and reduced phlebotomy burden; platelet increases, anemia, injection reactions, and continuing disease management still matter.

sections.title: From REViVE to VERIFY
sections.body: REViVE showed improved hematocrit control and reduced phlebotomy requirements, including a randomized withdrawal comparison. The phase 3 VERIFY study evaluated rusfertide added to ongoing standard care in adults requiring repeated phlebotomy. The approved label describes the controlled results supporting use; improvement in these endpoints is not the same as proof of curing PV.

sections.title: A current approval, not just a trial candidate
sections.body: FDA approved Mimrylo for erythrocytosis in adults with polycythemia vera on August 28, 2026. Earlier references correctly described development at their publication dates but are outdated if presented as current status. The indication remains specific to PV-related erythrocytosis rather than all disorders of iron or red-cell production.

sections.title: Platelets and anemia require attention
sections.body: Current labeling warns about new or worsening thrombocytosis and calls for blood-count monitoring. Injection-site reactions and anemia were common adverse reactions in the clinical program. Embryo-fetal toxicity is another warning. Hematocrit improvement therefore needs to be considered alongside platelets, symptoms, other PV therapy, and the overall treatment plan.

sections.title: Does it eliminate the need for other PV care?
sections.body: Not necessarily. The pivotal trial allowed ongoing standard treatment, and rusfertide targets erythrocytosis through iron regulation rather than removing the underlying neoplastic clone. A reduction in phlebotomy burden does not establish that every patient can stop cytoreductive therapy or that long-term thrombotic risk has been eliminated.

name: Selepressin
molecularClass: Synthetic selective vasopressin V1a-receptor agonist peptide
summary: Selepressin is an investigational vasopressin analog designed to emphasize vascular V1a-receptor activity. It was studied as an alternative pressor strategy in septic shock. The major SEPSIS-ACT trial stopped for futility and did not improve its primary patient-centered outcome, so a routine treatment role is unestablished.
description: Vasopressin affects both vascular tone and kidney water retention through different receptors. Selepressin was designed to favor the vascular V1a pathway and avoid some V2-mediated effects. This supplied a rationale for investigating whether more selective signaling could reduce organ support needs in septic shock. The development program progressed beyond small hemodynamic experiments to the adaptive SEPSIS-ACT randomized trial. That study tested a meaningful combined outcome of days alive and free of ventilation and vasopressors. Its negative result is central to the profile and cannot be replaced by an assumption that receptor selectivity must produce a clinical advantage over existing vasopressor care.
mechanism: Selepressin stimulates V1a receptors on vascular smooth muscle, increasing vascular tone through intracellular calcium signaling. Relative V1a selectivity was intended to separate pressor effects from V2-associated water retention and other vasopressin actions. However, a cleaner receptor profile does not automatically improve survival or organ recovery. Vasoconstriction may still alter regional perfusion, and the clinical consequence depends on illness, exposure, and concomitant treatment.
keyTakeaway: Selepressin remains an experimental vasopressor with a negative major outcome trial. Its receptor selectivity explains the development rationale but does not establish superiority, a survival benefit, or an approved alternative to vasopressin.

sections.title: What the adaptive trial found
sections.body: SEPSIS-ACT treated 828 participants and stopped after its first part for futility. Selepressin did not significantly improve ventilator- and vasopressor-free days compared with placebo added to background care. The trial also did not show significant benefit in key secondary outcomes including 90-day mortality or kidney-replacement-therapy-free days.

sections.title: Why the endpoint is more informative than pressure alone
sections.body: The protocol was designed to test whether a pressor strategy translated into less organ support while accounting for death. That is a broader clinical question than whether the drug can raise arterial pressure. The adaptive design allowed early termination when the probability of success was inadequate, limiting unnecessary further exposure.

sections.title: Selective receptors do not remove ischemic concerns
sections.body: Cardiac arrhythmia and ischemic events were monitored in the trial, including cardiac, mesenteric, and peripheral ischemia. Event comparisons did not establish a decisive clinical advantage. The monitored intensive-care setting and short exposure also limit conclusions about any unrelated outpatient or chronic use.

sections.title: Is it an approved replacement for vasopressin?
sections.body: No. The reviewed development program does not establish an approved US selepressin medicine or routine septic-shock indication. Vasopressin’s approval and familiarity cannot be transferred to this modified analog. Any future role would require new evidence addressing a specific population and clinically meaningful outcomes.

name: Cetrorelix
summary: Cetrorelix is an approved fertility medicine that prevents a premature luteinizing-hormone surge during controlled ovarian stimulation. It helps keep egg development and retrieval coordinated within an assisted-reproduction cycle; it is not a standalone treatment for every cause of infertility.
description: Cetrorelix is used by fertility specialists alongside medicines that stimulate ovarian follicle growth. Its job is to suppress the pituitary signal that could otherwise trigger ovulation before the planned egg-retrieval procedure. This distinction explains why a drug that temporarily lowers reproductive hormone signaling can support fertility treatment. The approved product is a subcutaneous injection, and its use is tied to ultrasound and hormone monitoring during a particular cycle. Pregnancy outcomes depend on the entire treatment pathway, including ovarian reserve, embryo development and other infertility factors, rather than on cetrorelix alone.
mechanism: Cetrorelix competitively blocks gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors on pituitary cells. This promptly reduces LH secretion and also affects FSH release. Unlike a GnRH agonist, it does not first stimulate a surge of pituitary hormones before suppression develops. The inhibition is reversible after treatment stops. In ovarian stimulation, externally supplied gonadotropins continue supporting follicle growth while the antagonist helps prevent an untimely endogenous LH surge.
keyTakeaway: Cetrorelix has an established, specific role in assisted reproduction: preventing an early LH surge. Successful hormone suppression does not guarantee pregnancy, and the medicine belongs within a monitored fertility protocol with other treatments.

sections.title: Why suppress LH during fertility treatment?
sections.body: A premature LH surge can disrupt the timing of egg maturation and retrieval. Cetrorelix inhibits that surge while ovarian-stimulation medicines support the follicles. It does not replace follicle-stimulating treatment or the separate intervention selected to trigger final egg maturation.

sections.title: What supports its clinical use?
sections.body: Randomized phase III research compared cetrorelix with established GnRH-agonist protocols during assisted reproduction. These studies, together with the prescribing-information trials, support control of premature LH surges. Their findings concern defined stimulation cycles, not improved natural fertility or treatment of low sex hormones outside that setting.

sections.title: Allergy and ovarian-stimulation risks
sections.body: Hypersensitivity, including serious systemic reactions, can occur. The label contraindicates treatment in pregnancy, lactation and severe renal impairment, and in patients with specified peptide-hormone or ingredient allergies. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome remains a concern within the overall stimulation cycle, requiring assessment by the treating fertility service.

sections.title: Is cetrorelix the same as an ovulation trigger?
sections.body: No. Cetrorelix suppresses the signal that could cause early ovulation; a trigger treatment has a different purpose later in the cycle. The timing of these separate steps is clinically consequential. Approved fertility use does not establish cetrorelix as a general hormone-balancing or anti-aging treatment.

name: Degarelix
summary: Degarelix is an approved androgen-deprivation medicine for advanced prostate cancer. It rapidly blocks pituitary GnRH signaling and lowers testosterone without the initial testosterone surge associated with GnRH agonists. Its established benefits concern cancer treatment, not general testosterone optimization.
description: Degarelix is supplied as Firmagon, a prescription injection that forms a depot after subcutaneous administration. Lowering testosterone can slow the growth of prostate cancers that remain dependent on androgen signaling. The choice of androgen-deprivation treatment depends on disease stage, other anticancer medicines, symptoms and the individual patient’s health. Degarelix is not chemotherapy and does not remove the need for further cancer-directed treatment when indicated. Testosterone and prostate-specific antigen measurements help assess its biological effect, while clinical evaluation and imaging address the broader course of the cancer.
mechanism: Degarelix binds directly to pituitary GnRH receptors as an antagonist. Blocking the receptor suppresses release of LH and FSH, and reduced LH stimulation lowers testosterone production by testicular Leydig cells. Receptor blockade acts without the initial stimulation produced by GnRH agonists. The drug therefore avoids an agonist-induced testosterone flare, although the longer-term consequences of androgen deprivation still apply.
keyTakeaway: Degarelix provides established testosterone suppression for advanced prostate cancer with rapid onset and no agonist flare. That pharmacologic advantage does not by itself prove better survival or cardiovascular safety than every alternative androgen-deprivation treatment.

sections.title: How does it fit into prostate-cancer care?
sections.body: The FDA indication is advanced prostate cancer. Degarelix provides the androgen-deprivation component of treatment; clinicians may combine this with other therapies according to the cancer’s characteristics. It is not a curative claim for all stages, and a falling PSA alone does not describe every aspect of response.

sections.title: What did the pivotal comparison establish?
sections.body: A randomized, open-label study enrolled 610 patients and compared degarelix with leuprolide over one year. Degarelix was noninferior for maintaining low testosterone and produced faster initial testosterone and PSA suppression. This endocrine endpoint should not be rewritten as a demonstrated survival advantage over leuprolide.

sections.title: What needs monitoring?
sections.body: Injection-site reactions and hot flushes are common. Hypersensitivity can be serious, and androgen-deprivation therapy can prolong the QT interval. The broader effects of sustained low testosterone include sexual and metabolic changes and loss of bone health, making clinical monitoring important beyond the injection itself.

sections.title: Does avoiding flare mean there are no hormone-related risks?
sections.body: No. Avoiding the initial testosterone rise is one difference from GnRH agonists. Degarelix still deliberately produces profound androgen deprivation, with associated symptoms and monitoring needs. Its approved oncology use does not support unsupervised use to adjust hormone levels or prevent disease in otherwise healthy people.

name: Ganirelix
summary: Ganirelix is an approved fertility-treatment peptide that prevents premature LH surges during controlled ovarian stimulation. It temporarily blocks pituitary GnRH receptors so the fertility team can coordinate follicle development and egg retrieval within a monitored assisted-reproduction cycle.
description: Ganirelix is used together with gonadotropins during ovarian stimulation. Its purpose is to prevent the body from initiating ovulation too early while multiple follicles are developing. Clinical protocols balance suppression of an unwanted LH surge against continued follicular growth, with ultrasound and hormonal assessment informing decisions. Ganirelix is distinct from the medicines used to stimulate the ovaries and from the final maturation trigger. Although it can support the timing of IVF or related procedures, it does not resolve every cause of infertility or independently guarantee a successful pregnancy.
mechanism: Ganirelix competitively antagonizes the GnRH receptor on pituitary gonadotroph cells. This produces rapid, reversible suppression of LH and FSH secretion without first stimulating the receptor. In a fertility cycle, externally administered FSH supports the ovaries while ganirelix limits premature endogenous LH release. Its mechanism is related to cetrorelix, but the molecules and their individual prescribing instructions are not identical.
keyTakeaway: Ganirelix has a well-established role in controlling premature LH surges during assisted reproduction. It is one component of a carefully timed fertility cycle, and its approved use should not be generalized to routine hormone suppression or enhancement.

sections.title: What does ganirelix contribute to an IVF cycle?
sections.body: Ganirelix helps preserve the planned timing of egg maturation and retrieval by suppressing an early LH surge. It is not itself an ovarian-stimulation medicine. The relevant outcome is safe coordination of the complete treatment cycle, rather than maximal suppression of every reproductive hormone.

sections.title: What human evidence supports it?
sections.body: A multicenter randomized phase III trial compared ganirelix with a long leuprolide protocol during controlled ovarian hyperstimulation. The clinical program evaluated premature LH surges, ovarian response, pregnancy outcomes and tolerability. These data support the approved reproductive setting and do not establish benefit for unrelated hormone or wellness goals.

sections.title: What are the main precautions?
sections.body: Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, require attention. Known or suspected pregnancy and relevant GnRH-related allergies are contraindications. Some needle shields may contain natural rubber or latex, depending on the product. Injection-site symptoms can occur, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome must still be monitored within the broader stimulation protocol.

sections.title: Can ganirelix and cetrorelix simply be swapped?
sections.body: Both block GnRH receptors, but a shared drug class does not make individual fertility schedules interchangeable. Product instructions and the timing of ovarian stimulation remain specific. Changes during a cycle require the fertility team’s assessment because incomplete suppression can interfere with planned egg retrieval.

name: Goserelin
molecularClass: Synthetic GnRH agonist peptide in a biodegradable implant
summary: Goserelin is an approved GnRH-agonist implant that suppresses sex-hormone production after an initial stimulation phase. Depending on the formulation and indication, it is used in prostate cancer, advanced breast cancer, endometriosis and preparation for endometrial ablation.
description: Goserelin is delivered through a subcutaneous implant that releases medicine over time. Sustained suppression of testosterone or ovarian estrogen can treat conditions driven by these hormones. The US Zoladex label includes defined prostate-cancer settings, palliative treatment of advanced breast cancer in premenopausal or perimenopausal women, endometriosis and endometrial thinning before ablation. Different implant presentations do not necessarily share every indication. Temporary ovarian suppression is a treatment effect rather than proof of permanent infertility, and neither absent menstruation nor suppressed hormone measurements should be treated as reliable contraception.
mechanism: Goserelin initially activates pituitary GnRH receptors and briefly increases gonadotropin secretion. With continuous exposure, the pituitary response becomes suppressed, lowering LH and FSH and consequently testosterone or estradiol. This two-stage agonist effect differs from immediate receptor blockade by antagonists. Reduced sex-hormone signaling explains both activity against hormone-sensitive disease and adverse effects such as hot flushes and bone mineral loss.
keyTakeaway: Goserelin has established hormone-suppressing uses in oncology and gynecology. Its initial flare, longer-term bone and metabolic effects, implant procedure and indication-specific treatment limits matter as much as its ability to lower hormone levels.

sections.title: Which uses are established?
sections.body: The label includes advanced prostate cancer and a specified regimen with flutamide and radiotherapy for certain prostate tumors. Other indications include advanced breast cancer in premenopausal or perimenopausal women, endometriosis, and endometrial thinning before ablation. Treatment purpose and duration differ across these conditions.

sections.title: Why does disease context matter?
sections.body: Randomized clinical research has studied goserelin alone and with tamoxifen in advanced breast cancer. Those findings concern hormone-sensitive cancer populations and combinations. The current label describes separate evidence for prostate and gynecologic indications; one study cannot be used as a blanket efficacy estimate for all of them.

sections.title: What risks accompany sustained suppression?
sections.body: Initial tumor flare can worsen symptoms in prostate cancer. Other concerns include reduced bone density, hyperglycemia, cardiovascular risk, QT prolongation, depression and pregnancy-related harm. Implant administration can cause serious injection-site injury or bleeding. These risks require assessment according to the patient’s condition and treatment setting.

sections.title: Is goserelin a permanent way to switch off hormones?
sections.body: Its intended pharmacologic action is reversible suppression, although recovery varies with age, exposure and underlying disease. It should not be assumed to provide contraception. In endometriosis, the label limits the established treatment course because prolonged estrogen deprivation raises additional concerns, including bone loss.

name: Histrelin
molecularClass: Synthetic GnRH agonist peptide delivered by subdermal implant
summary: Histrelin is a GnRH agonist that provides prolonged suppression of pituitary and gonadal hormone signaling through an implant. The current US Supprelin LA product is approved for children with central precocious puberty, following appropriate diagnostic assessment.
description: Histrelin illustrates how continuous exposure to a hormone agonist can ultimately suppress the pathway it first stimulates. Supprelin LA releases histrelin from an implant placed under the skin and is used for central precocious puberty, where the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes active unusually early. Treatment aims include slowing pubertal progression and excessive advancement of bone age. Implant placement and removal are clinical procedures, and biochemical response and growth require follow-up. The separate prostate-cancer implant Vantas is listed as discontinued in current FDA records; its historical indication should not be substituted for the current pediatric implant label.
mechanism: Following an initial increase in LH, FSH and sex steroids, continuous histrelin exposure desensitizes the pituitary response to GnRH. Lower gonadotropin output reduces ovarian estrogen and testicular testosterone production. In central precocious puberty, this suppresses the early activation of the normal pubertal pathway. It does not address every cause of early sexual development, which is why hormone-independent disorders must be distinguished during diagnosis.
keyTakeaway: Histrelin is an established specialist treatment for confirmed central precocious puberty. The implant’s long action does not remove the need for hormone, growth and bone-age monitoring or for careful placement and complete removal.

sections.title: Why must the cause of early puberty be confirmed?
sections.body: Central precocious puberty results from premature activation of the GnRH pathway. The label requires a diagnostic evaluation that includes hormone testing and bone-age assessment, with imaging or additional tests as appropriate. Histrelin does not automatically treat hormone secretion arising independently from the pituitary pathway.

sections.title: What did the pediatric trial show?
sections.body: A prospective multicenter study enrolled 36 children and evaluated a histrelin implant over one year. Stimulated LH and sex-steroid concentrations were strongly suppressed, supporting the treatment’s endocrine effect. Longer-term growth and clinical follow-up remain important because hormone suppression is not identical to a guaranteed adult-height outcome.

sections.title: What monitoring and procedure risks matter?
sections.body: An early hormonal flare can transiently increase pubertal symptoms. The implant can be difficult to locate or remove and may break, requiring confirmation that all fragments are removed. Label warnings also address psychiatric symptoms, convulsions, severe skin reactions and pediatric intracranial hypertension.

sections.title: Does an implant mean treatment can be left unattended?
sections.body: No. The labeled pathway includes planned follow-up, assessment of LH and sex-steroid suppression, and tracking of growth and bone age. Placement and removal require appropriate procedural care. A long-acting formulation changes delivery convenience, not the need to verify that treatment is achieving its intended effect.

sections.title: Is the adult Vantas implant still marketed?
sections.body: Current FDA records list Vantas as discontinued. This is a separate presentation from Supprelin LA, which remains labeled for central precocious puberty. The historical adult oncology indication does not make the pediatric implant an interchangeable prostate-cancer product; formulation, availability and the applicable label must be distinguished.

name: Human chorionic gonadotropin
molecularClass: Glycoprotein hormone composed of alpha and beta subunits
summary: Human chorionic gonadotropin is a large reproductive hormone with approved medical uses in selected infertility and hormone-deficiency conditions. It activates the LH receptor and can support ovulation or testicular testosterone production. It has no established benefit as a weight-loss treatment.
description: hCG is naturally produced during pregnancy, but pharmaceutical hCG is used for specific reproductive indications. The US Pregnyl label includes ovulation induction in selected anovulatory infertility, certain cases of male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and selected prepubertal cryptorchidism without an anatomical obstruction. These are distinct clinical situations requiring assessment of the underlying cause. Urine-derived hCG and recombinant chorionic gonadotropin products have their own formulations and labeling. hCG acts directly on the gonads, so its effects differ from GnRH medicines that act mainly through the pituitary. A raised testosterone measurement alone does not establish improved fertility.
mechanism: hCG binds the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor. In testicular Leydig cells, receptor activation stimulates steroid production, including testosterone. In the ovary, it can trigger final follicular maturation, ovulation and luteinization after appropriate follicular development. Its alpha and beta protein subunits and attached carbohydrate groups distinguish this glycoprotein from short synthetic research peptides. Receptor activity does not make it an effective fat-loss hormone.
keyTakeaway: hCG is an established prescription hormone for selected reproductive conditions, with clinically significant risks and monitoring requirements. Its fertility and endocrine evidence does not support hCG diets, obesity treatment or general claims of improved performance.

sections.title: Which indications are actually approved?
sections.body: Pregnyl is labeled for selected anovulatory infertility after appropriate ovarian stimulation, certain male hypogonadotropic-hypogonadism cases, and selected prepubertal cryptorchidism not caused by anatomical obstruction. The diagnostic category matters: stimulating the gonads cannot reliably correct primary ovarian failure or every cause of infertility.

sections.title: What does the evidence not support?
sections.body: The prescribing information explicitly rejects hCG as an effective adjunct for obesity. FDA also warns against hCG weight-loss products. Changes associated with severely restricted diets do not establish a drug effect on fat distribution, appetite or durable weight control.

sections.title: What are the main treatment risks?
sections.body: In ovarian stimulation, hCG can contribute to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, which can become severe, and multiple pregnancy is a concern. Thromboembolic events, fluid retention, gynecomastia and precocious puberty are among relevant risks. Treatment requires condition-specific monitoring rather than interpretation of a single hormone number.

sections.title: Is hCG equivalent to testosterone replacement?
sections.body: No. hCG stimulates LH receptors and can increase endogenous testicular testosterone when responsive tissue is present; testosterone replacement supplies the hormone directly. Their effects on fertility and feedback signaling differ. Whether hCG is appropriate depends on diagnosis, and evidence for one labeled indication does not validate every combined hormone regimen.

name: Leuprolide
molecularClass: Synthetic GnRH agonist peptide; formulation-specific depot medicines
summary: Leuprolide is an established GnRH agonist used to suppress sex-hormone production. Different approved products serve advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, selected preoperative fibroid-related anemia and central precocious puberty. Its formulations and indications must be distinguished rather than treated as interchangeable.
description: Leuprolide is a synthetic analogue of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, supplied in several injection and depot formulations. Continuous exposure initially stimulates and then suppresses pituitary signaling, reducing testosterone or ovarian estrogen. The same biological action is useful in several diseases, but treatment objectives differ: controlling androgen-dependent cancer, reducing endometriosis symptoms, improving anemia before fibroid surgery with iron, or suppressing early central puberty. Product labels differ in delivery, duration, population and permitted combinations. A label for a prostate-cancer depot therefore cannot be assumed to describe a pediatric or gynecologic preparation.
mechanism: Leuprolide activates pituitary GnRH receptors, initially increasing LH and FSH release. Sustained exposure then desensitizes the pituitary response and reduces gonadotropin secretion, lowering gonadal sex steroids. The initial stimulation can cause a temporary symptom flare before suppression occurs. Longer-term hypoestrogenism or androgen deprivation explains several adverse effects, including hot flushes, sexual symptoms, bone loss and relevant metabolic changes.
keyTakeaway: Leuprolide has multiple established indications, but each belongs to a specific product and clinical pathway. Hormonal flare, bone health, metabolic effects and treatment duration require attention; shared active ingredient does not make different depots interchangeable.

sections.title: Which product is intended for which condition?
sections.body: US labels separately describe prostate-cancer Lupron Depot, pediatric Lupron Depot-PED and gynecologic Lupron Depot. The fibroid indication concerns preoperative hematologic improvement with iron in patients with bleeding-related anemia. Endometriosis labeling addresses symptom control and, in specified circumstances, norethindrone add-back therapy.

sections.title: How should benefits be interpreted?
sections.body: The prescribing information reports clinical studies for the relevant formulation and indication. Testosterone suppression is a key prostate-cancer endpoint; pediatric assessment includes stimulated hormone responses, pubertal progression and growth; gynecologic studies evaluate symptoms, lesions or anemia. These outcomes should not be collapsed into a general claim of hormone optimization.

sections.title: What risks differ across treatment settings?
sections.body: Tumor flare can worsen prostate-cancer symptoms early in treatment. Labels address bone loss, pregnancy-related harm, psychiatric effects, seizures and severe skin reactions. The prostate label also covers metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and QT effects; pediatric labeling includes intracranial hypertension. Monitoring should follow the actual product and population.

sections.title: Does add-back therapy cancel the intended effect?
sections.body: In approved endometriosis regimens, norethindrone add-back is used to reduce certain consequences of estrogen suppression, including bone loss, while treating symptoms. This does not mean every leuprolide use needs the same combination. The gynecologic label specifies limits on duration and circumstances for retreatment.

name: Lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan
molecularClass: PSMA-targeted radioactive small-molecule ligand with a peptide-like binding motif
summary: Lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan, marketed as Pluvicto, delivers targeted radiation to PSMA-expressing prostate cancer. Its US indications expanded in July 2026 to include selected metastatic hormone-sensitive disease with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor, in addition to defined resistant-disease settings.
description: Pluvicto combines a PSMA-binding ligand, a metal-binding chelator and the radioactive isotope lutetium-177. It is a radioligand cancer medicine rather than a conventional hormone peptide. Patient selection requires an appropriate PSMA-positive imaging assessment and attention to disease stage and previous therapy. The current US label covers metastatic androgen pathway modulation-naïve or sensitive disease with an ARPI, and specified resistant disease after an ARPI. The latter includes patients considered suitable to delay taxane chemotherapy or previously treated with a taxane. It is administered by teams equipped for radiopharmaceutical treatment and radiation protection.
mechanism: The ligand binds prostate-specific membrane antigen on target cells. Lutetium-177 then emits beta radiation that damages DNA in PSMA-expressing cells and nearby tissue, potentially causing cell death. PSMA expression is not exclusive to tumor tissue, so targeting does not eliminate exposure of normal organs. Renal elimination, bone-marrow effects and cumulative radiation exposure remain clinically relevant despite the treatment’s molecular targeting.
keyTakeaway: Pluvicto is an approved targeted radioligand with indication-specific randomized evidence and an expanded 2026 US label. Eligibility depends on PSMA imaging and treatment history, and progression benefits must be distinguished from demonstrated survival results in each trial population.

sections.title: How did the indication change in 2026?
sections.body: FDA approved Pluvicto with an ARPI for adults with PSMA-positive metastatic androgen pathway modulation-naïve or sensitive prostate cancer, previously termed metastatic hormone-sensitive disease. The resistant-disease indication also remains: previous ARPI therapy plus suitability to delay taxane chemotherapy or prior taxane treatment.

sections.title: Which outcomes have been demonstrated?
sections.body: VISION established progression and overall-survival benefit in a previously treated resistant-disease population. PSMAfore supported earlier use before taxane chemotherapy through improved radiographic progression-free survival; its overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. PSMAddition supported the 2026 hormone-sensitive indication through improved radiographic progression-free survival. These populations and endpoints are different.

sections.title: What does targeted radiation still put at risk?
sections.body: The label warns about cumulative radiation exposure, severe myelosuppression, kidney toxicity, embryo-fetal harm and male infertility. Fatigue, dry mouth and nausea are among common adverse effects. Blood counts, kidney function and radiation-protection procedures are integral to treatment rather than optional additions.

sections.title: Is a PSMA scan the treatment itself?
sections.body: No. PSMA imaging helps identify suitable disease and select patients, while Pluvicto delivers therapeutic radiation. A positive scan alone does not establish eligibility without the relevant clinical and treatment-history criteria. The radiopharmaceutical must be handled in an appropriately equipped clinical service.

name: Nafarelin
molecularClass: Synthetic decapeptide GnRH agonist administered intranasally
summary: Nafarelin is an approved nasal GnRH-agonist medicine used for endometriosis and central precocious puberty. Continuous treatment suppresses pituitary-gonadal hormone signaling after an initial stimulation phase. Its nasal route does not make its systemic hormonal effects mild or purely local.
description: Nafarelin, marketed as Synarel, provides a noninjectable route for sustained suppression of reproductive hormone signaling. The US label covers central precocious puberty in children of either sex and management of endometriosis, including pain and lesions. The endometriosis experience described in the label is in adults treated for a limited course. Successful treatment depends on consistent absorption and follow-up, not merely possession of a nasal spray. Diagnosis is particularly important in children because early sexual development can have causes outside the central GnRH pathway, which require different investigation and treatment.
mechanism: Nafarelin stimulates pituitary GnRH receptors at first, briefly increasing gonadotropins and sex steroids. With repeated exposure, pituitary responsiveness declines, suppressing LH and FSH and lowering ovarian estrogen or testicular testosterone. This can reduce estrogen-driven endometriosis activity or pause premature central pubertal progression. The same mechanism can produce hot flushes, vaginal symptoms and bone effects, even though administration is through the nose.
keyTakeaway: Nafarelin is an established systemic hormone-suppressing medicine delivered by nasal spray. Its approved uses require diagnosis, monitoring and attention to treatment duration; nasal delivery does not remove GnRH-agonist risks or establish general fertility-enhancement benefits.

sections.title: What conditions does the US label cover?
sections.body: For endometriosis, nafarelin is used to relieve pain and reduce lesions; the label describes experience in adults over a limited treatment course. For central precocious puberty, diagnosis requires evidence that the central reproductive pathway is active and exclusion of other causes of early development.

sections.title: What supports the endometriosis indication?
sections.body: A multicenter double-blind trial compared nasal nafarelin with oral danazol. Both treatments reduced endometriosis manifestations, with differing adverse-effect patterns. This evidence addresses treatment of established endometriosis rather than a claim that suppressing reproductive hormones improves fertility in people without that diagnosis.

sections.title: What should be assessed during treatment?
sections.body: The label addresses initial hormonal flare, loss of bone mineral density, pregnancy-related harm and hypersensitivity. Pediatric monitoring includes growth and biochemical suppression; warnings also cover psychiatric events, convulsions and intracranial hypertension. Nasal conditions and other intranasal medicines can affect practical administration and should be considered.

sections.title: Does lack of menstruation mean reliable contraception?
sections.body: No. Suppression of menstruation is a treatment effect, not assurance that pregnancy cannot occur. Nafarelin is contraindicated during pregnancy, and the label calls for appropriate pregnancy prevention. Likewise, an apparently convenient nasal route does not justify extending endometriosis treatment beyond the evidence and label limits.

name: Oxytocin
molecularClass: Cyclic nonapeptide hormone and uterotonic medicine
summary: Oxytocin is a naturally occurring nine-amino-acid hormone and an established obstetric medicine. Approved injectable products help initiate or strengthen suitable labor contractions and control postpartum uterine bleeding. Claims about routine enhancement of bonding, mood or social behavior require separate evidence.
description: Natural oxytocin participates in uterine contraction and milk ejection, while pharmaceutical oxytocin is used in monitored maternity care for specific obstetric purposes. The US injectable label includes medically indicated labor induction, selected augmentation of labor, adjunctive management of incomplete or inevitable abortion, and production of uterine contractions to control postpartum bleeding. Appropriate use depends on maternal and fetal assessment and whether vaginal delivery is suitable. Intranasal oxytocin investigated for behavioral or psychiatric effects is a separate research context; the established obstetric record does not automatically validate those applications or an unapproved compounded formulation.
mechanism: Oxytocin activates oxytocin receptors on uterine smooth-muscle cells, engaging intracellular signaling that increases calcium and promotes contraction. Uterine sensitivity varies with pregnancy and clinical context. After delivery, contraction helps compress uterine blood vessels and limit bleeding. At higher or prolonged exposure, oxytocin’s antidiuretic activity can also influence water balance, contributing to the risk of water intoxication and low sodium.
keyTakeaway: Oxytocin has established obstetric uses with substantial monitoring needs. Evidence for labor and postpartum bleeding should remain separate from experimental intranasal or behavioral uses, where a natural-hormone mechanism has not consistently translated into clinical benefit.

sections.title: Where is oxytocin established?
sections.body: The injectable label describes medically indicated induction or reinforcement of suitable labor and control of postpartum uterine bleeding. It also includes adjunctive management of incomplete or inevitable abortion. Suitability depends on the obstetric situation; circumstances requiring surgical delivery or making vaginal delivery unsafe are important contraindications.

sections.title: Does the obstetric evidence prove behavioral benefit?
sections.body: No. A 24-week placebo-controlled trial in 290 children and adolescents with autism found no significant advantage for intranasal oxytocin on the primary social-withdrawal measure. This result does not erase oxytocin’s obstetric utility; it shows that effects depend on route, population and clinical outcome.

sections.title: Why is monitoring essential?
sections.body: Excessive uterine activity can compromise fetal oxygenation and can cause serious maternal injury, including uterine rupture. Prolonged administration can cause water intoxication, hyponatremia and seizures. Appropriate assessment of contractions, fetal status, fluid balance and the overall maternal condition is fundamental to safe clinical use.

sections.title: Is a “bonding hormone” label a treatment indication?
sections.body: No. A hormone’s physiological role does not establish that administering it improves relationships, sexual function, mood or social behavior. Those questions require their own controlled studies and product-specific evaluation. Approved injectable oxytocin for obstetric care should not be presented as approval of intranasal wellness products.

name: Triptorelin
molecularClass: Synthetic decapeptide GnRH agonist in long-acting formulations
summary: Triptorelin is an approved GnRH-agonist medicine that suppresses gonadal hormone production after an initial stimulation phase. US products include Trelstar for advanced prostate cancer and Triptodur for central precocious puberty in children aged two years and older.
description: Triptorelin is used in separate oncology and pediatric formulations with different clinical objectives. In prostate cancer, lowering testosterone reduces stimulation of androgen-dependent disease. In central precocious puberty, suppression of early gonadotropin activation slows premature pubertal progression. Although the active peptide is shared, the product, formulation, labeled population and follow-up requirements are specific. Depot delivery maintains prolonged exposure and cannot be understood as an occasional physiological GnRH pulse. Additional triptorelin products and indications exist outside the United States; local labeling should be checked rather than assuming a brand name carries identical uses everywhere.
mechanism: Triptorelin initially stimulates pituitary GnRH receptors, increasing release of LH and FSH. Continued exposure then suppresses receptor responsiveness and gonadotropin secretion, reducing testosterone or ovarian estrogen. This delayed suppressive action produces an early flare that differs from the immediate blockade of GnRH antagonists. The eventual fall in sex steroids explains both therapeutic action and consequences such as hot flushes and effects on bone health.
keyTakeaway: Triptorelin is an established hormone-suppressing medicine for specific oncology and pediatric indications. The same peptide in different depot products is not interchangeable without clinical review, and treatment response requires more than simply observing reduced hormone levels.

sections.title: How do the approved products differ?
sections.body: Trelstar is labeled for advanced prostate cancer. Triptodur is labeled for central precocious puberty in pediatric patients aged two years and older. The distinction involves more than packaging: the populations, treatment goals, formulation instructions and monitoring endpoints differ and must follow the relevant prescribing information.

sections.title: What did comparative prostate-cancer research show?
sections.body: A randomized study of 284 men compared triptorelin with leuprolide. Both maintained low testosterone effectively, although initial suppression developed at different rates. The trial supports the drug’s androgen-deprivation effect; its results should not be generalized into a definitive claim that triptorelin is superior for long-term cancer survival.

sections.title: What risks are important in adults and children?
sections.body: An early flare can worsen prostate-cancer symptoms. Adult labeling also addresses metabolic and cardiovascular risks, QT prolongation and seizures. Pediatric labeling includes psychiatric symptoms and intracranial hypertension. Severe skin reactions are another GnRH-agonist concern. Follow-up must assess the individual disease, hormonal response and adverse effects.

sections.title: Can the prostate-cancer and pediatric depots be substituted?
sections.body: A shared active ingredient does not make these preparations interchangeable. They have distinct formulation and indication instructions. In children, clinical and biochemical confirmation of central precocious puberty is essential; in adults, androgen suppression must fit the broader prostate-cancer plan and symptom assessment.

name: Kisspeptin-10
molecularClass: Ten-amino-acid kisspeptin fragment and KISS1 receptor agonist
summary: Kisspeptin-10 is a short reproductive-signaling peptide studied in human endocrine physiology. Small experiments show that it can stimulate LH and sometimes testosterone, but this does not establish an approved treatment for infertility, low libido or testosterone deficiency.
description: Kisspeptin-10 is the active ten-amino-acid end of the kisspeptin family encoded by KISS1. It acts upstream of GnRH and is useful for studying how the brain regulates reproduction. Human research includes brief controlled exposure in healthy men and a small study in men with type 2 diabetes and mild biochemical hypogonadism. These studies examine hormone secretion rather than long-term clinical outcomes. The wider kisspeptin literature also includes kisspeptin-54 and other analogues, which must not be treated as interchangeable evidence for this exact fragment or for products sold outside clinical research.
mechanism: Kisspeptin-10 activates KISS1R, historically called GPR54, on the reproductive neuroendocrine pathway. This can stimulate GnRH secretion and subsequently pituitary LH and FSH release, with downstream effects on gonadal hormone production. Response depends on exposure pattern and the physiological state of the axis. A short-lived rise in LH demonstrates biological activity but does not by itself establish sustained improvement in fertility, symptoms or sexual function.
keyTakeaway: Kisspeptin-10 has credible human evidence of endocrine activity but no established approved therapeutic indication. Its small physiology studies, uncertain long-term safety and differences from kisspeptin-54 limit claims about fertility, libido or testosterone treatment.

sections.title: What has kisspeptin-10 shown in people?
sections.body: A controlled study in healthy men demonstrated increased LH secretion and changes in LH pulsatility during intravenous kisspeptin-10 exposure. A separate small study in men with type 2 diabetes and mild biochemical hypogonadism showed LH and testosterone responses. Neither establishes durable symptom improvement or a fertility treatment.

sections.title: Are sexual-desire trials evidence for this fragment?
sections.body: Some frequently cited sexual-processing and desire studies administered kisspeptin-54. For example, a randomized study in women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder used that longer peptide. Such results can inform the broader pathway but should not be relabeled as trials of kisspeptin-10.

sections.title: What is known about safety and product quality?
sections.body: FDA identifies potential immunogenicity, peptide-impurity and active-ingredient-characterization concerns for compounded kisspeptin-10. Available safety information for proposed administration routes is inadequate. Short research exposures cannot establish the safety of repeated use, different routes, pregnancy exposure or products with uncertain identity and purity.

sections.title: Does a rise in LH mean fertility has improved?
sections.body: No. Hormone secretion is an intermediate biological measurement. Fertility depends on many additional factors, and meaningful evidence would include outcomes such as sperm production, ovulation or live birth in appropriate populations. Kisspeptin-10 remains investigational rather than an FDA-approved fertility or libido medicine.

name: Gonadorelin (compounded)
molecularClass: Synthetic form of the native decapeptide gonadotropin-releasing hormone
summary: Gonadorelin is synthetic GnRH, a hormone that stimulates pituitary LH and FSH release when delivered in an appropriate pulsatile pattern. Historical US human products are discontinued, and compounded preparations are not FDA-approved. Fertility evidence is specific to diagnosed deficiencies and treatment methods.
description: Gonadorelin reproduces the native ten-amino-acid hypothalamic hormone rather than a long-acting GnRH analogue. Pulsatile delivery has been studied for selected patients whose reproductive hormone deficiency originates in the hypothalamus, provided pituitary and gonadal function can respond. Historical US products included Factrel and Lutrepulse Kit; FDA product records list both applications’ products as discontinued. A compounded preparation does not inherit those products’ approval or establish equivalence to a study’s drug and delivery system. Veterinary gonadorelin products are separate medicines and are not evidence of current approval for human treatment.
mechanism: GnRH binds receptors on pituitary gonadotroph cells and stimulates LH and FSH secretion. The timing of stimulation is central: physiological pulses sustain gonadotropin output, while prolonged continuous stimulation can desensitize the pathway. Consequently, results from a pulsatile delivery system cannot be assumed for an unrelated intermittent regimen. Response also depends on the site of the underlying defect; a damaged pituitary or gonad may not respond normally.
keyTakeaway: Gonadorelin has meaningful reproductive physiology and selected clinical evidence, but compounded products remain unapproved. Historical approval, veterinary availability and results from specialized pulsatile treatment should not be used as interchangeable proof for current wellness or testosterone-therapy claims.

sections.title: What does the human fertility evidence show?
sections.body: A clinical study treated 11 men with idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism using prolonged pulsatile GnRH. Eight developed spermatogenesis on GnRH alone, with another responding after additional gonadotropin treatment. The selected population and specialized delivery method limit extrapolation to other causes of infertility or unrelated hormone regimens.

sections.title: What happened to the historical US medicines?
sections.body: FDA records for Factrel, application 018123, and Lutrepulse Kit, application 019687, list their human products as discontinued. These records document past approved products, not approval of a new compounded preparation. The fact that an active ingredient has a regulatory history does not approve every formulation containing it.

sections.title: What remains uncertain with compounded preparations?
sections.body: Compounded medicines do not undergo FDA premarket verification of safety, effectiveness and quality. Concentration errors, contamination and product consistency are relevant concerns. For gonadorelin, clinical response also requires the correct diagnosis and delivery pattern; a hormone increase alone does not confirm successful spermatogenesis or pregnancy benefit.

sections.title: Does pulsatile GnRH evidence prove fertility preservation during testosterone therapy?
sections.body: No. Research in men with hypothalamic hormone deficiency is not the same clinical question as adding a compounded product to testosterone treatment. The evidence cited here does not establish that an arbitrary intermittent regimen preserves fertility. Both the underlying diagnosis and the actual treatment method must match the supporting evidence.
